desc:
You are given k non-empty lists of integers, each sorted in non-decreasing order. Find the smallest closed range [lo, hi] that contains at least one element from every list.

Range [p, q] is smaller than range [r, s] if q - p < s - r, or if q - p == s - r and p < r. Return the answer as the two-element array [lo, hi].

lists = [[4, 10, 15, 24, 26], [0, 9, 12, 20], [5, 18, 22, 30]]
result = [20, 24]

The range [20, 24] contains 24 from the first list, 20 from the second and 22 from the third, and no range of length 4 or less does better.
constraints: 1 ≤ each list length, and the total number of elements is at most 6,000
Each list is sorted in non-decreasing order
hints: Try to think of all the elements pooled into one array, with each element remembering which list it came from. A candidate range then becomes a window of that array.
Sort the pooled elements by value. You are looking for the shortest window (in value span) that contains at least one element of each of the k lists, like the minimum window substring problem.

Expand the right edge of the window one element at a time while counting how many distinct lists are present. Whenever all k lists are present, record [value at left, value at right] if it beats the best (smaller span, then smaller lo), then shrink from the left while keeping all lists covered.
editorial: Label every element with its list index and sort the pairs (value, list); a range [lo, hi] corresponds to a contiguous window of this sorted array. The question becomes: what is the window with the smallest value span that includes every list label at least once? This is the same sliding-window technique as the smallest substring that contains all required characters.

Move the right edge forward, maintaining count[list] and the number of lists with a non-zero count. While that number equals k, compare the span of the current window against the best (smaller span wins, ties go to the smaller lo), then drop the left element and update the counts. Both edges move only forward, so after sorting the sweep is linear. Total time is O(N log N) for N elements; a heap holding one element of each list gives O(N log k) without sorting everything up front, and works the same way (always advance the list whose current element is the smallest).
solution:
def smallestRange(lists):
    k = len(lists)
    items = sorted((v, i) for i, lst in enumerate(lists) for v in lst)
    count = [0] * k
    covered = 0
    best = None
    left = 0
    for right in range(len(items)):
        li = items[right][1]
        if count[li] == 0:
            covered += 1
        count[li] += 1
        while covered == k:
            lo, hi = items[left][0], items[right][0]
            if best is None or (hi - lo, lo) < (best[1] - best[0], best[0]):
                best = [lo, hi]
            lj = items[left][1]
            count[lj] -= 1
            if count[lj] == 0:
                covered -= 1
            left += 1
    return best
